body:
> 🤖 Generated by the Agentic Engineer

### Motivation

#2790 removes a construct that makes an assertion report the wrong answer. Nothing stops it coming
back — it is the obvious way to write such a check, and it had already been fixed once at a single
site and then reintroduced 73 times.

Fixing this class also surfaced a live defect in the telemetry the Agent Improver scores runs from:
the same fault in its scope filter was discarding **every** session that took place inside a
submodule, so improvement decisions were being made from roughly the monorepo-root sessions only.
The existing tests could not have caught it — each one exercised a simplified case in exactly the
dimension the fault lives in, which makes a test blind rather than merely weak.

### What this changes

Adds a check that rejects the construct in CI, fixes the telemetry scope defect, and clears the
remaining occurrences. The check is covered by its own tests, including a demonstration of the
underlying fault and controls in both directions.

Worth flagging for later: the same construct exists in the submodules, which this check cannot see.
The right fix is to publish it as a shared building block rather than to point this repo's check at
other repositories — filed separately.

author: hanzala-afzal-dev
body:
Before this, engine.run() built a new DuckDB database for every query and closed it again at the end. That cost is the same every time, a few milliseconds, whatever the query does. It is paid once per call at all 47 call sites, so it grows with the number of queries and not with the size of the data. A full pytest run spent about a third of its time on it, across roughly 1700 queries.

Now the process keeps one instance and each call takes a cursor on it. Calls stay just as separate as they were before, which is what makes this safe. Every call still gets its own cursor, the frames it registers live in that cursor only, and they are gone when it closes, so no call can ever see what another call registered.

The instance is built when the first query runs, not when the module is imported, so importing retentioneering and running nothing costs no time and no memory. A lock stops two threads from building it twice.

An os.register_at_fork handler keeps the instance that a child process got from its parent, instead of dropping it. If it dropped the last reference, Python would close that instance, and closing one that the parent still uses is the thing we must avoid. The child builds its own on its next query. The handler also replaces the lock, because only the thread that called fork() lives on in the child, and a lock that another thread held at that moment would stay locked for ever.

Adds tests/engine/ for cursor isolation, which is what the whole change rests on, plus the late build, one instance under a thread race, and the fork handler with a real fork on POSIX.

<!-- Thanks for contributing to retentioneering! Keep the PR focused on one logical change. -->

## What & why

`engine.run()` built a new DuckDB database for every query and closed it again at the end. That cost is the same every time, a few milliseconds, whatever the query does, so it grows with the number of queries and not with the size of the data. Now the process keeps one instance and each call takes a cursor on it.

Improvement discussed here #115 

## Before / after

Before: every call opened a database, registered the frames, ran the query and closed the database.
After: one instance for the whole process, one cursor per call.

Query path on my machine, median of 7 runs of 30 queries, duckdb 1.5.5:

| rows | before | after | faster by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 1252 ms | 270 ms | 4.6x |
| 10000 | 1255 ms | 447 ms | 2.8x |
| 100000 | 1451 ms | 751 ms | 1.9x |
| 500000 | 7237 ms | 3572 ms | 2.0x |

Results are the same before and after. I checked this on 1k, 50k and 250k rows, on a query joining two frames, and on a query using a reserved word as a column name.

## What & why

`engine.run()` built a new DuckDB database for every query and closed it again
at the end. That cost is the same every time, a few milliseconds, whatever the
query does, so it grows with the number of queries and not with the size of the
data. Now the process keeps one instance and each call takes a cursor on it.

Discussed in #115.

## Before / after

Before: every call opened a database, registered the frames, ran the query and
closed the database.
After: one instance for the whole process, one cursor per call.

Query path on my machine, median of 7 runs of 30 queries, duckdb 1.5.5:

| rows | before | after | faster by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 1252 ms | 270 ms | 4.6x |
| 10000 | 1255 ms | 447 ms | 2.8x |
| 100000 | 1451 ms | 751 ms | 1.9x |
| 500000 | 7237 ms | 3572 ms | 2.0x |

Results are the same before and after. I checked this on 1k, 50k and 250k rows, on a query joining two frames, and on a query using a reserved word as a column name.

What stays private to a call is the frames it registers. They live in that call's cursor, they are gone when it closes, and one of them always wins over a stored object of the same name. Other connection state is not private any more, see the first note below.

The instance is built when the first query runs, not at import, so importing retentioneering and running nothing costs no time and no memory. A lock stops two threads from building it twice. After a `fork()` the child moves the instance it got from the parent aside instead of dropping it, so the close does not happen while the parent is still using it, and the child builds its own on its next query.

Tested on Linux with Python 3.12 and 3.13: 1315 passed, 1 skipped. I also broke the code on purpose in five ways, one at a time, and checked that the tests catch each one.

## Notes for review

- **One behaviour change through the `sql=` hatch.** If a query stores something in the catalog, for example `CREATE TABLE` or `CREATE VIEW`, that object used to die with the connection and now stays for the life of the process. If the string ends in a SELECT, no error reaches the caller either. The docstrings ask for a SELECT, so this was never supported, and it cannot produce wrong answers: a frame that a call registers always wins over a stored object of the same name. There is a test for that
- **The fork handler also replaces the lock.** Only the thread that calls `fork()` lives on in the child. If another thread held the lock at that moment, it would stay locked for ever and the child would hang on its first query. Two lines, with a test. Note that moving the instance aside only delays the close, it does not prevent it: at shutdown Python clears module globals and the destructor runs then.
- **Small correction on parallel queries.** `rete.mcp.serve()` starts the server on a background thread in `mcp/server.py`, so an agent can query while the user runs a cell. Queries in parallel are possible today. That is an argument for the lock, not against the change.

## Checklist

- [x] Ran `make install-dev` (one-time per clone) so the git hook is active
- [x] `uv run pre-commit run --all-files` passes (ruff lint + format, hygiene, gitleaks) — this is CI's `lint` job

- [x] Sync obligations handled where applicable (MCP tool layer, JS metric editor / widget contract)

I ran `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` manually with version 0.8.6, the one pinned in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, and both pass.

Also, the docstring is updated. `render_pages.py` reads `Eventstream` docstrings and `engine` is not one of them, so there was nothing to rebuild.

Regarding sync obligations, nothing public changed, so the MCP layer and the JS metric editor are untouched.

author: stservice
body:
# PR Summary — Issue #538 ## Summary `loss.rs` gains two **additive** public items so consumers stop re-implementing MSE around the core kernels. Closes #538. - **`mse_record(targets, outputs) -> f64`** — the per-record reduction (mean over outputs of `(target - output)^2`, accumulated in `f64` and scaled by the reciprocal of `outputs.len()`), exported for callers that already hold their activations and cannot use a fused batch path — the NEAT-AI-Backpropagation trace pass. `0.0` when `outputs` is empty. The scalar `mse_sum_batch_packed` closure and the `mse_mean_record` closure now **delegate** to it; they were the same maths written twice. The SIMD tile kernels (`interleaved_tile_mse`, `mse_sum_batch_scattered`) read strided/interleaved buffers and are bit-parity-critical, so they are untouched. - **`mse_mean_streaming(network, dir, input_size, num_outputs, forward_only, max_records) -> Result<(f64, u64), String>`** — streams a `.bin` training directory through the shared `for_each_read_chunk` scan, buffers each chunk into a packed `[inputs…, targets…]` batch, and reduces it with the existing `mse_sum_batch_packed` so the SIMD 8/4-way fast path still does the work. A record straddling a chunk or file boundary is carried in a residual buffer. `max_records` truncates the batch in flight, so a capped pass costs no extra I/O. `forward_only = false` routes through the non-fused reset-per-record path, preserving stateless semantics. Both are re-exported from `lib.rs`. `mse_mean_streaming` is deliberately **not** on the `#[cfg_attr(target_arch = "wasm32", wasm_bindgen)]` export surface — it is a native-host convenience, not a JS/WASM boundary call (it still compiles for `wasm32`, verified below). No existing signature changed. ### Edge-case decisions - A directory with no `.bin` files, a missing directory, or a corpus holding no whole record returns `(0.0, 0)` — the issue puts the fail-loud decision with the caller. - A trailing incomplete record **after** at least one whole record is an `Err` naming the dangling byte count, rather than being silently dropped. - I/O failures from listing or reading the corpus propagate unchanged. ## Evidence Backend/library change — no web interface to screenshot. Evidence is the test suite plus the mutation results below. ```mermaid flowchart LR D[".bin directory"] --> L["find_bin_files"] L --> R["for_each_read_chunk"] R --> P{"whole records
in buffer?"} P -- "partial" --> B["residual buffer
carried to next chunk"] B --> P P -- "yes" --> K["mse_sum_batch_packed
SIMD 8/4-way per chunk"] K --> C{"max_records reached?"} C -- no --> R C -- yes --> M["mean = Σ per-record MSE / N"] R -- "corpus drained" --> M ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A["mse_sum_batch_packed
scalar path"] --> X["mse_record"] B2["mse_mean_record"] --> X C2["mse_mean_streaming"] --> K2["mse_sum_batch_packed"] K2 --> X D2["external consumers
(backprop trace pass)"] --> X E["interleaved_tile_mse
mse_sum_batch_scattered"] --> Y["own bit-parity-critical
reductions — untouched"] ``` Commands run (all with `< /dev/null`): - `./quality.sh` → **All quality checks passed** (fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, deny, full workspace tests, docs, release build). - `cargo test -p neat-core` → 181 lib + every integration target green, including the pre-existing bit-parity suites `mse_batch_interleaved_parity`, `mse_squash_simd_parity`, `packed_record_scan`, `inline_squash_dispatch` and `aggregate_squash_tail_parity` — unchanged, so the fused numerics were not perturbed. - `cargo check -p neat-core --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` → clean (the `wasm32` target is not gated on PRs; `loss.rs` is compiled for it). ### Mutation evidence The delegation is a collapse of two copies, so each former site was shown to be reachable. Mutating `mse_record`'s return to `sq_sum * inv_outputs + 0.1` and running the targets that isolate each former site: | Former site | Isolating target | Result under mutation | | --- | --- | --- | | `mse_mean_record`'s closure | `cargo test -p neat-core --lib mse_mean_record` | **RED** — 2 failed (`mse_mean_record_matches_hand_rolled_reference`, `..._agrees_with_sum_divided_by_records_on_forward_only`) | | `mse_sum_batch_packed`'s scalar closure | `cargo test -p neat-core --test mse_squash_simd_parity` | **RED** — 4 failed (scalar reference vs fused SIMD parity) | | new public surface | `cargo test -p neat-core --test mse_mean_streaming` | **RED** — 7 failed | The mutation was reverted before commit (`sq_sum * inv_outputs` is the only form left in `mse_record`; the four other `sq_sum * inv_outputs` occurrences are the untouched SIMD tiles). ## Test Plan New file `neat-core/tests/mse_mean_streaming.rs` (14 tests). Its primary oracle is **independent** of the batched kernels (AGENTS.md rule 1): `reference_mean` activates each record on its own through `CompiledNetwork::activate` and averages hand-computed squared errors. Fixtures shard the byte stream into files whose lengths are deliberately not multiples of the 20-byte record, so records straddle every file/chunk boundary and the residual buffer is exercised. - `mse_mean_streaming_matches_single_record_reference` — 23 records over 4 non-aligned shards equals the independent per-record reference. - `mse_mean_streaming_equals_packed_sum_over_records` — the issue's acceptance criterion: equals `mse_sum_batch_packed(...) / num_records`. - `mse_mean_streaming_recurrent_route_matches_reference` — `forward_only = false` (reset-per-record) matches the same reference. - `mse_mean_streaming_empty_directory_returns_zero` and `mse_mean_streaming_directory_with_no_whole_record_returns_zero` — `(0.0, 0)`. - `mse_mean_streaming_missing_directory_yields_no_records` — `(0.0, 0)`. - `mse_mean_streaming_max_records_truncates_deterministically` — caps 1/5/8/17 each score exactly that many records and match the mean over the first N. - `mse_mean_streaming_max_records_above_corpus_scores_everything` and `mse_mean_streaming_zero_max_records_scores_nothing`. - `mse_mean_streaming_trailing_partial_record_is_an_error` — 6 dangling bytes after 3 whole records fails loud, naming the byte count. - `mse_record_is_the_mean_squared_difference`, `mse_record_single_output_is_the_squared_difference`, `mse_record_empty_outputs_returns_zero` — derived expected values, not vacuous assertions. - `packed_batch_reduces_one_record_through_mse_record` — one record through `mse_sum_batch_packed` equals `mse_record` of that record's targets against the single-record activation, asserted with `assert_eq!` (bit-for-bit), which is the behavioural evidence that the scalar path reduces through the shared helper. Docs updated in the same change: a **Streaming directory MSE (Issue #538)** section in `README.md` (with the flow diagram above) and the Issue #444 section of `AGENTS.md`, which now records that MSE's reduction is the exported `mse_record` and that the SIMD tiles keep their own. --- 🤖 Processed by: VibeCoderST 🏷️ Run id: `vibe-msqldu5l-ee0332`

author: mrutunjay50
body:
The release run failed after 9m23s with "failed to decode secret key: incorrect updater private key password: Missing comment in secret key". Signing is the last thing tauri-action does, so every mistyped secret costs a full build to discover, and the message names the password when the actual problem is the key.

Check both secrets in the first step instead. It fails in seconds and says which of the specific ways the value can be wrong applies: blank, whitespace or a line break, not base64, base64 twice, truncated, or the public half pasted by mistake. Neither the key nor the password is ever printed - only the character count and which check tripped.

The value is checked untrimmed, and any whitespace at all is rejected. That looks over-strict but matches what actually happens: Tauri decodes this with Rust's base64, which refuses whitespace, while .NET's FromBase64String quietly accepts it. Trimming here - the obvious thing to write - would wave through a secret with a trailing newline and let it fail in the build nine minutes later, which is precisely the failure this step exists to prevent. A single trailing newline is enough.

Verified against thirteen mutations of the real key: only the exact file contents pass, and each mutation is caught by the check that names it. The key itself is fine - it signs correctly when passed as contents rather than a path, which is how CI passes it.

author: ronaldlokers
body:
**Stacked on #572.** Not a shell bug — an older one the shell's new column led me to.

## What happened

I was checking whether `board_folded` (#547) survives the nightly backup. It does: the queries are `SELECT *`, so **columns look after themselves**. But that raised the neighbouring question — what about *tables*? The backup and the user-facing export both walk a hand-written list.

So I wrote a test comparing the schema against that list. It found **six tables holding user data in neither the backup nor the export**:

| Table | What is lost |
|---|---|
| `journal_entries` | **prose the user wrote** |
| `saved_views` | named board filters |
| `webhooks` | configured endpoints |
| `feed_ats_boards` | configured job boards |
| `feed_company_blocklist` | companies muted from the feed |
| `notifications` | history and read state |

**Nothing said so.** The export succeeded every time — it just didn't contain them. The failure only surfaces when someone restores and finds their journal gone.

All six are `user_id`-scoped, so they slot into the per-user export as well as the full backup.

## The test is the durable part

A table added in a migration and forgotten here now **fails** rather than quietly falling out of the backup. Tables deliberately excluded — Better Auth's own, encrypted third-party keys, device-bound push subscriptions — are listed with the reason, so omission stays a decision rather than an oversight.

The other direction is covered too: a renamed or dropped table would leave the export querying something gone, which throws at 3am with nobody watching.

## Verification

- The test fails on the pre-fix list (that's how the six were found) and passes after
- `npx tsc -b`, `oxlint` (exit 0), `npm run build` — clean
- `npx vitest run --no-file-parallelism` — **672/672**, 105 files

## Description
  - **What changed**: When a subpackage deleted from upstream is in the unfetched state in origin (only contains a Kptfile), the update logic now fetches the full origin content at the correct commit SHA before performing the diff against local.
  - **Why it's needed:** Previously, the diff between an unfetched origin (bare Kptfile) and local (full fetched content) always showed differences, so the subpackage was never deleted even when the user had made no local changes.
  - **How it works:** The `updatePackage` function in `pkg/lib/update/update.go` detects the unfetched origin state via `pkg.IsPackageUnfetched()`, reads the commit SHA from the local `upstreamLock`, fetches origin at that exact commit using a new `Commit` field on `fetch.Command`, adds merge comments, and then performs the diff as before.

This PR is based on #2230, which was authored against the old codebase structure (when packages lived under `internal/`). That PR was never merged. These changes port the same approach to the current codebase (packages now under `pkg/lib/`) with adapted API signatures and additional test coverage.

author: felipelorenz
body:
https://liferay.atlassian.net/browse/LPD-75968

Stacked on #2115.

## What Is Being Fixed

`WorkflowMetricsReindexer` was registered as a Liferay-only SPI, so the seven workflow-metrics reindexers were invisible to Liferay Search's generic `IndexReindexer` (i.e. Search Admin's per-index reindex). The reindex lifecycle — index drop and recreate — was owned by `WorkflowMetricsReindexBackgroundTaskExecutor` and duplicated per reindexer, and `WorkflowMetricsIndex.deleteAllDocuments` was a dead code path that predated the drop-and-recreate approach.

## How It Is Being Fixed

All seven reindexers now register under both `IndexReindexer` and `WorkflowMetricsReindexer` (`service = {IndexReindexer.class, WorkflowMetricsReindexer.class}`), so the reindexers are reachable from Search Admin.

`BaseWorkflowMetricsReindexer` is a new abstract template method for the five entity reindexers (`Instance`, `Node`, `Process`, `Task`, `Transition`). It owns the FULL lifecycle: the `!isWorkflowMetricsSupported || SYSTEM` guard, `removeIndex + createIndex`, and a call into a `reindexEntities(long, ExecutionMode)` abstract method the subclasses implement. Follow-up PRs add `createMissingIndexes` on top of this skeleton (PR 3) and the SYNC branch (PR 4).

The two SLA reindexers (`SLAInstanceResult`, `SLATaskResult`) dual-SPI without extending `BaseWorkflowMetricsReindexer`. Their pre-migration behavior — `_createDefaultDocuments` plus, on `SLAInstanceResult`, `WorkflowMetricsSLAProcessBackgroundTaskHelper.addBackgroundTasks(true)` — is unchanged because their indexes are populated asynchronously; putting them on the drop-and-recreate FULL lifecycle would clash with the async recalc. Their `reindex(long, ExecutionMode)` implementation delegates to `reindex(long)` regardless of mode.

`WorkflowMetricsReindexBackgroundTaskExecutor` loses the old `deleteAllDocuments` loop and its three `@Reference` fields (`IndexNameBuilder`, `SearchCapabilities`, `SearchEngineAdapter`), since the base now owns the lifecycle. `WorkflowMetricsIndex.deleteAllDocuments` and its adjacent imports (`DeleteByQueryDocumentRequest`, `QueriesUtil`) are removed as orphaned. `settings.json` gains `"index.default_pipeline": "timestamp"` on the workflow-metrics indexes. `source-formatter.properties` adds the reindexer directory to `allowedMultipleServiceTypesClassNames` so `JavaComponentAnnotationsCheck` accepts the dual-SPI registration. `portal-workflow-metrics-service/build.gradle` picks up a `portal-search-spi` compile-only dep.

A `Rename` commit fixes long-standing `creatDefaultDocument` typos across the two SLA indexers and their two consumers (`NodeWorkflowMetricsIndexerImpl`, `ProcessWorkflowMetricsIndexerImpl`).

## Why Are There No Tests?

The behavior contract PR 2 introduces — that seven reindexers register under both SPIs and go through a shared FULL lifecycle — is exercised by the existing integration test bundle in `portal-workflow-metrics-test`, which resolves the reindexers by key and drives them through the executor. PR 3 adds a new integration test (`WorkflowMetricsReindexerTest`) that asserts every reindexer creates its missing indexes; that test lives with the `createMissingIndexes` PR because the assertion depends on the new hook.

author: klebermdc
body:
Front da etapa 1.1 do módulo de Marketing. Depende de `klebermdc/chat-bullq-api#180` (já mergeado).

Sem este PR a API do Marketing existe mas **não há como conectar uma conta** — não existe tela.

## O que entra

- `src/features/settings/services/meta-ads.service.ts` — cliente HTTP das 5 rotas de `/marketing/connections`
- `src/app/(dashboard)/settings/meta-ads/page.tsx` — tela de conexão
- Aba "Meta Ads" em Configurações

Só frontend. `npx tsc --noEmit` limpo, `npm run build` ok.

## Detalhes que valem a revisão

**O fluxo tem dois passos porque o código OAuth é de uso único.** O passo 1 manda o `code`; a API troca uma vez, guarda `{token cifrado, contas}` no Redis sob um `handshakeId` (TTL 10 min, leitura destrutiva) e devolve `{handshakeId, accounts}`. O passo 2 manda `{handshakeId, adAccountId}`. **O token nunca chega ao navegador** — não existe campo de token em lugar nenhum do código do front.

**`FB.login` é chamado de forma síncrona no clique.** O SDK é pré-carregado num `useEffect` no mount, porque qualquer `await` entre o clique e o `FB.login` faz o navegador bloquear o popup em silêncio. Mesmo padrão do `create-channel-dialog.tsx` do Embedded Signup.

**Handshake expirado reseta a tela.** Se o passo 2 falhar, o seletor de contas é limpo e o usuário volta ao "Conectar", em vez de ficar clicando num botão morto ligado a um `handshakeId` já consumido.

**Conexão quebrada é impossível de não ver.** Token do Meta dura ~60 dias e a renovação exige o usuário. Quando morre, `status` vira `INVALID_TOKEN` ou `REVOKED` → card com borda vermelha, selo dizendo para reconectar, e o `lastSyncError` da API renderizado literalmente. Isso é resposta direta ao histórico de integração que parou em silêncio.

## Antes de funcionar

`NEXT_PUBLIC_META_ADS_APP_ID` e `NEXT_PUBLIC_META_ADS_CONFIG_ID` precisam estar no `.env` **e** na lista `environment:` do serviço `web` no compose — e o web precisa ser **rebuildado**, porque `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` é cozido no build, não lido em runtime. Sem isso a tela carrega e o botão avisa que falta configuração.

- `Choice` — 사진 박스 `height: 320px` → `aspect-ratio: 171 / 320`
- `Tile` — `height: 124px` → `aspect-ratio: 111.33 / 124`

사진이 들어가는 두 컴포넌트는 높이 고정 대신 비율 고정으로 바꿨습니다. 폭이 변해도 사진이 가로로 퍼지지 않고, 나중에 `object-fit: cover` 로 실제 사진을 채울 때 잘리는 영역이 화면 크기와 무관하게 일정해집니다.

**화면 규격 통일 (14개 페이지)**

- `max-width` → **450px** 로 통일. 기존에는 430px 12개, 402px 1개, 390px 1개로 섞여 있었습니다. 현재 가장 넓은 기기가 440px(iPhone 17 Pro Max)이라, 450이면 모든 기기에서 좌우 여백이 의도한 24px로 유지됩니다.
- 좌우 패딩 → **24px** 로 통일. 20px이던 4개 화면(`Home`, `TripArchive`, `TripManagement`, `TripSegmentEdit`)과 0이던 `LogIn` 을 맞췄습니다.
- `LogIn` 은 래퍼에 24px를 주면서 `TitleArea` 에 중복으로 있던 `padding: 0 24px` 를 제거했습니다.

---

## 🖥️ 테스트 방법

1. `npm run dev`
2. 브라우저 개발자도구에서 기기 폭을 **375 / 402 / 440px** 로 바꿔가며 확인
3. `/onboarding/basic-question` — 선택지가 본문 폭을 꽉 채우고 좌우 여백이 24px로 유지되는지
4. `/onboarding/ab-preference` — A/B 카드가 폭에 따라 비율을 유지하며 커지는지 (찌그러지지 않는지)
5. `/login` — 구글 로그인 버튼이 좌우 24px 안쪽에 놓이는지
6. `/permission` — 권한 카드가 본문 폭을 꽉 채우는지
7. `/`, `/archive`, `/trip-management` — 좌우 여백이 다른 화면들과 같은지

---

## 📝 참고 사항 (미진행 / 후속 논의)

- **`LogIn` 의 버튼이 더 이상 화면 끝까지 닿지 않습니다.** 피그마 로그인 화면에서는 버튼 폭이 390(화면 전체)이라 원래는 좌우로 꽉 찬 디자인이었는데, 패딩 통일로 24px씩 들어왔습니다. 의도와 다르면 되돌려야 합니다.
- **`PhotoCapture`, `PinSaveComplete` 는 패딩 통일에서 제외했습니다.** 각각 카메라 뷰(검은 화면 풀블리드), 상단 바·구분선이 화면 끝까지 이어지는 구조라 좌우 패딩 0이 의도된 것으로 봤습니다. `max-width` 는 450으로 함께 맞췄습니다.
- **`Tile` 은 아직 어느 화면에도 적용되지 않았습니다.** 무드보드 화면이 402px 기준으로 다시 그려지면 그때 붙일 예정입니다. 3열 그리드 간격은 `column-gap: 10px` (354 = 111.33 × 3 + 10 × 2), 세로 간격은 미확정입니다.
- **테두리 두께 차이로 인한 레이아웃 밀림은 그대로 남아 있습니다.** `Option` 은 선택 시 1px 커지고 `Choice` 의 하단 태그는 2px 줄어듭니다. 피그마는 테두리를 안쪽에 그리지만 CSS `border` 는 바깥으로 쌓이기 때문입니다. 디자인 확인 후 `box-shadow: inset` 으로 정리할 예정입니다.
- **디자인 기준 폭은 402px, 구현 최대 폭은 450px 입니다.** 402px보다 넓은 화면에서는 본문이 피그마보다 비례해서 커집니다. 컴포넌트를 전부 비율·100% 기반으로 바꿔놔서 레이아웃은 깨지지 않지만, 피그마와 픽셀 단위로 비교하면 차이가 납니다.

author: b3nw
body:
## Thinking Path

The kanban board already renders a short task ID on every card
(`.kanban-card-id` in `_kanbanCard`) and the bridge serializes the full Task
dataclass (`asdict(task)` in `api/kanban_bridge.py`), so the complete task ID is
already available client-side on every card and in the edit modal's fetched
task. The gap was purely on the surface: there was **no way to copy the full ID**
for pasting into the CLI, search, links, or parent-dependency fields. The task
ID is a "copy somewhere" value — it belongs on the card next to the short ID and
in the edit modal, each behind a one-click copy action. Because the value is
already in the payload and already rendered, this is a display/interaction-only
change with no server or agent involvement.

## What Changed

- **Kanban cards** (`static/panels.js` → `_kanbanCard`, `copyKanbanTaskId`):
  a small copy icon button now sits in the card's top line next to the task-ID
  span. Clicking it copies the full task ID to the clipboard via the existing
  `_copyText` helper. The handler calls `event.stopPropagation()` so the click
  does **not** also open the task detail view (the card `<article>` keeps its
  `onclick`/`onkeydown`/`draggable` attributes intact), and swaps the icon to a
  check for 1500 ms as feedback, falling back to a `copy_failed` toast.
- **Edit-task modal** (`static/index.html` → `#kanbanTaskModalIdRow`,
  `static/panels.js` → `copyKanbanTaskModalId`, `_kanbanSetTaskModalLabels`):
  a new read-only Task ID row with a one-click copy button. It is revealed only
  in edit mode (`_kanbanSetTaskModalLabels('edit')`) and populated with the real
  task id by `openKanbanEdit`; create mode keeps it hidden because a new task has
  no ID yet.
- **CSS** (`static/style.css`): additive rules for the card copy button
  (`.kanban-card-copy`) and the modal ID row + copy button
  (`.kanban-modal-id-display/-value/-copy`, plus a `.copied` feedback state),
  all using existing CSS variables.
- **i18n** (`static/i18n.js`): added `kanban_task_id` and `kanban_copy_task_id`
  to **all 15 locale blocks** to satisfy `test_kanban_locale_parity`; the copy
  feedback reuses the existing global `copied` / `copy_failed` keys.

## Why It Matters

There was no ergonomic way to retrieve a kanban task ID from the UI — users had
to dig it out of the card/detail text manually or the CLI. This adds a
finding-a-ID affordance (copy icon on each card) and an editing-a-ID affordance
(copyable ID in the edit modal), so pasting a task ID into the `kanban` CLI,
search, links, or the parent-dependency field is one click.

## Verification

- Kanban static + bridge suites: `./scripts/test.sh tests/test_kanban_ui_static.py tests/test_kanban_bridge.py -q` → **95 passed**.
- New tests added: `test_kanban_card_has_copy_task_id_affordance`,
  `test_kanban_edit_modal_id_row_shown_only_in_edit_mode` — both assert the
  feature markers and were verified to fail against upstream `master`.
- The repo's pre-push gate passed: 0 ruff findings, no whitespace/conflict
  issues, correct co-author trailer.
- **Browser UAT** on a staging instance (read-only — no task state mutated):
  - Card copy: clicking the card's `.kanban-card-copy` button on a test card
    copied the task ID to the clipboard, and did **not** open the task detail
    (`detailOpened: false`) — stopPropagation verified.
  - Edit-modal ID row: opening Edit revealed the read-only Task ID row
    (`idRowShown: true`, value = the task id); its copy button copied the ID
    with check-icon `.copied` feedback. Modal closed via Cancel.
  - Visual confirmation: the card copy icon renders next to the task ID on the
    top line, and the edit modal's Task ID row renders as a monospace value with
    a copy button. (Screenshots available on request.)

## Risks / Follow-ups

- Low. The change is additive (new DOM/CSS/tests; nothing existing modified)
  and display-only — it cannot corrupt agent state or spawn workers.
- The card copy button adds a small visual element to every card top line; the
  icon is muted until hover so it reads as an affordance without competing with
  the summary text. If maintainers prefer, the icon size/placement can be
  adjusted to match the project's icon language.
- No Agent-side change needed; `task.id` already flows through the bridge.

## Model Used

- Claude (Anthropic Opus 5) for codegen and test completion.
- A Gemini-based pre-PR code review (verdict: no issues found).

author: mronkko
body:
Three independent correctness fixes on the write path. Each is self-contained
and separately revertable; none depends on the others.

### 1. `attach_mode` now means what its description says

`attach_mode="none"` still downloaded and attached OA PDFs. The parameter was
threaded through the add path but never consulted at the point that actually
fetches the PDF, so the only thing it changed was the reported status string.
Callers asking for metadata-only imports got full PDF downloads.

### 2. Batch tag/extra updates retry on HTTP 412

`batch_update_tags` and `batch_update_extra` read an item, mutate it, and PUT it
back. Anything that bumps the item's version in that window — a sync, a
concurrent edit, Zotero itself — makes the PUT fail with 412 and the update is
silently lost for that item. Adds a bounded re-fetch/re-apply/re-send retry,
matching the pattern already used elsewhere in the file.

### 3. A rate-limited read no longer masquerades as data

pyzotero returns the HTTP 429 error body as `bytes` from every read method
instead of raising, so a throttled read looks like a successful one. Iterating
bytes yields ints, so callers get a list of integers where item dicts should be:

```
_helpers.py  find_existing_items
  AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'get'
```

`len()` reports the body's byte count as a plausible-looking result count, so
nothing looks wrong until something dereferences an entry.

The path through pyzotero 1.13.4:

1. `errors.error_handler` special-cases 429 — it records the server-supplied
   backoff and returns instead of raising, documented as "leaving the caller to
   retry".
2. No caller retries. `_post_check` just returns, so the 429 response is handed
   back as if the request had succeeded.
3. `retrieve` then dispatches on the *response* `Content-Type`. Zotero sends
   `text/plain` for error bodies, which matches none of the JSON/Atom/BibTeX
   branches and falls through to `return retrieved.content`.

The fix has two halves, and the second is the one that does the work.

First, `_ZoteroClient`: a pyzotero subclass whose `_retrieve_data` reissues a
429'd read instead of returning it. Retrying is what `error_handler`'s docstring
already assumes — the backoff is recorded by the time it returns, and
`_check_backoff` sleeps for exactly that duration at the start of the next
request, so a bounded loop needs no timing logic of its own. After N attempts it
raises `ZoteroRateLimitedError`.

Second, the three client factories — `get_zotero_client`,
`get_local_zotero_client`, `get_web_zotero_client` — now construct that subclass
instead of `zotero.Zotero`. This reads like incidental tidying, but without it
the fix does nothing: an override only applies to instances of the subclass, so
while the factories keep handing back a plain `zotero.Zotero`, every client in
the process stays unguarded. Those factories are the only places a client is
constructed, which is what lets one change cover every read in the codebase — 87
call sites that would otherwise each need to recognise a `bytes` response on
their own. Nothing else about the client changes.

`find_existing_items` needs more than not-crashing. Every failure there degrades
to "no match" so the caller creates the item — right for a genuinely failed
search, but a throttled search hasn't answered the question, and reading it as
"not present" silently creates duplicates of items that are. It now lets rate
limiting propagate.

Filed upstream as urschrei/pyzotero#352, since any pyzotero consumer is exposed
to this.

`_ZoteroClient` is a workaround, but how it can be retired depends on the shape
of the upstream fix, so it carries a TODO saying so. If pyzotero retries
internally, the class is redundant and deletes cleanly. If pyzotero instead
*raises* on a rate-limited read, deleting it would reintroduce the bug by
another route: `super()._retrieve_data` would raise before the status check,
losing the retry, and `_is_rate_limited` wouldn't recognise pyzotero's own
exception class — dropping it back into the "treat as no match" path that
silently creates duplicates.

`test_rate_limit_guard.py` pins unguarded pyzotero's behaviour directly, so it
starts failing as soon as an installed version changes it, and the dependency
comment in `pyproject.toml` points at the TODO for whoever raises the floor.

### Testing

`1681 passed` on this branch. Each fix ships with regression tests
(`test_v021_fixes.py`, `test_version_conflict_retry.py`, `test_rate_limit_guard.py`).

author: nomyfan
body:
An approval could go unanswered forever, or be applied to the wrong batch of tool calls. Reported from a forked session: the first batch was approved and ran, the second was approved too — but the first batch's rows turned into "rejected", the second batch never happened, and refreshing or restarting the server changed nothing. Only deleting the forked session cleared it.

Two independent bugs produced that together.

## The resume never reached the thread

`bootstrap` found the thread to resume through the runtime snapshot's `active_threads`. That snapshot is only written when an agent exits, so it says nothing about a session that never exited cleanly — a process killed mid-approval, or a session a fork has just minted (`fork_session` copies checkpoints and messages, and rightly leaves the source's runtime state behind). The lookup found nothing, the decision was never consulted, and it was dropped without a warning. The thread stayed parked, every later approval was swallowed the same way, and only deleting the session helped.

A decision already knows which thread it answers — the pending approvals it covers come from the *checkpoints* — so it now carries that thread (`ResumeTarget`) and resumes on it directly, falling back to the snapshot only for agents with no decision.

Since #44 that is not enough on its own: `register_resumed_work` restores a turn only for threads the snapshot named, so a decision-routed resume would run with an empty active slot — a task submitted alongside it would open a second turn, and an abort would find nothing to mark. The turn is now restored from the checkpoint each decision names. A decision for an agent the team no longer has is dropped first, so no turn is restored that nothing can close.

## The resume answered the wrong batch

A decision answers one batch, and a call it does not name counts as rejected — so a decision meant for an earlier batch rejects the batch actually parked, with "Rejected by user" going back to the model. A second submit of the same approval (a double click, a retry after a reconnect, a decision buffered during shutdown and replayed) is enough to get there.

The batch is identified by the assistant message that asked for it — `parent_message_id`, which `PendingApproval` already knew, now travels to the client and comes back on the `ResumeDecision`. A mismatch is ignored and the real suspension re-announced, so the client resynchronizes.

Call ids are deliberately **not** consulted for this: an id is only unique within one assistant message, which this codebase has settled twice already — the `twice-main` fixture reuses one on purpose, and #44 minted `call_envelope_id` per dispatch rather than trust `call_id`. A first attempt here did use call ids and failed both ways: with a provider that numbers ids per assistant message a stale decision looked live and was applied to the wrong batch, while a decision that deliberately names nothing (relying on "an unnamed call is rejected" to refuse everything) was mistaken for stale and ignored.

The web client also drops a second submit of an approval whose first is still in flight, so the duplicate is not sent at all.

## Wire change

`PendingApproval` and `ResumeDecision` each gained `parent_message_id`. Note that `ResumeDecision` is serialized into `runtime_snapshots`, so a stored snapshot holding a buffered `Resume` envelope will no longer deserialize — acceptable per the project's stance on persisted formats, but worth knowing when reopening old sessions.

## Testing

Verified manually against the original forked-session repro. Every fix is also covered by a test confirmed to fail without it:

- `an_approval_resumes_a_session_that_never_wrote_a_runtime_snapshot`
- `a_resume_without_a_snapshot_puts_the_interrupted_turn_back`
- `a_resume_meant_for_an_earlier_batch_does_not_reject_the_current_one` — both batches now share a call id, so the discarded call-id heuristic cannot pass it
- `an_empty_decision_for_the_parked_batch_rejects_it`
- `a second submit of the same approval while one is in flight is dropped` (web)

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` and `cargo test --workspace` are clean; `pnpm --filter coda-web` lint / typecheck / test all pass.

## Known remaining imprecision

`drop_stale_envelopes` keeps a replayed `Resume` whenever its thread is parked on *any* `PendingApproval`, without comparing the batch — unlike the `Reply` arm beside it, which matches `call_envelope_id` exactly. The driver's batch check already prevents any damage, so this is consistency rather than correctness, and is left for a follow-up.

author: zitch-systems
body:
Two reported bugs and one requested change.

## 1. The app stopped at the splash screen

Reported as "zitch mobile app not opening": the navy screen with the Z mark,
held indefinitely.

Nothing in `app/_layout.tsx` guaranteed the splash would ever lift.
`SplashScreen.hideAsync()` ran only on `fontsLoaded`, and the effect above it did
`if (error) throw error` — so a font that failed to load threw **before** the
splash was hidden, and the app never opened. If the load neither resolved nor
rejected, the early `return null` held it forever with no deadline.

Fonts may now delay the first paint and never prevent it: loaded, failed, or four
seconds elapsed all open the app (in the system face if it must), and
`hideAsync` / `preventAutoHideAsync` rejections can no longer surface as a boot
crash. The rule lives in `lib/boot.ts` with its truth table as the test.

**Second defect on the same path.** The session-lock effect called
`router.replace("/signin")` on the first commit — the `return null` one, with no
navigator mounted. expo-router refuses that, and from an un-awaited async
function it became an unhandled rejection with the lock bounce silently dropped,
so a locked session could land on the home screen. Now gated on `ready`, with the
async errors contained.

## 2. The bot ignored details the customer had already given

Reported as "ai did not recognise the chat and the user had to start the
transaction from scratch". One message —
`Load my nepa bill. 2000010657 5,000 to IKEDC` — was answered with "Which
disco?", then "Prepaid or postpaid?".

`dispatch_intent`'s `pay_bill` branch called `_start_electricity(user, msisdn)`
with no arguments, discarding `biller`, `customer_id` and `amount`, while the
`buy_airtime` branch directly above forwards its slots. The model had extracted
all three.

- The electricity flow is driven by what it still does not know, so a detail
  already given is never asked for twice.
- `IKEDC` and its eight siblings resolve to their disco — at the prompt too, not
  only through the model.
- `nepa` deliberately resolves to nothing: it means electricity, not a company,
  and guessing a disco from it would put the wrong meter in front of a payment.
- Cable gets the same treatment for its provider and smartcard.

Pre-filling decides which **questions** are asked, never which **checks** run:
the meter is still verified with the provider, the amount still passes the
minimum/balance/limit checks, and it still ends at the same confirm + PIN.

## 3. Requested: transaction timeouts

Two clocks, from one `_flow_deadline(state)` helper every flow-creating path
routes through:

| State | Window |
|---|---|
| Armed, waiting for the PIN (chat PIN/SMS code **and** the secure Flow's PIN pad) | **1 minute** |
| Still collecting details | **5 minutes** |

The Flow endpoint already refused an expired action, so a PIN pad left open past
the window submits into nothing. Timeouts also stopped being silent: expired
flows were deleted on the next read, so a payment mid-confirm simply vanished —
the customer is now told what expired and that nothing was charged, and a message
that isn't a PIN still gets its normal answer.

**Worth a decision:** 1 minute is tight for the secure Flow path (tap the card,
wait for the native form, type 6 digits). One line — `PIN_TTL` in `router.py` —
if 90s or 2 minutes is preferred.

## Tests

- App: typecheck and lint clean; 92 pass, 5 new covering the boot invariant.
- Backend: 411 WhatsApp tests pass, 13 new — the pre-filled bill end to end, the
  one remaining question when prepaid/postpaid is absent, PIN still required,
  disco aliases at the prompt, `nepa` naming no disco, the unverifiable-meter
  path, cable, both timeout windows, the arm-time clock change, and the expiry
  notice. Full backend suite re-running on the rebased base.

Rebased onto `main` after #329 merged, so this branch carries only the new work.

author: turneraroundauto-hub
body:
## Summary
- Reported live: DRAM (Roundhill Memory ETF) kept showing "No SEC CIK found" in Pre-Gate, even though it has a real, findable CIK.
- Researched via web search — this sandbox's egress proxy blocks `sec.gov` outright (confirmed via `curl` 403 and `WebFetch` `EGRESS_BLOCKED`), so I could not fetch SEC's files directly to inspect them. What I found: **DRAM = Roundhill Memory ETF**, launched Apr 2, 2026, registered under **Roundhill ETF Trust, CIK 1976517** — confirmed via SEC's own EDGAR filing URLs referencing DRAM directly (an 8-A Cert PDF under `/Archives/edgar/data/1976517/.../8A_Cert_DRAM.pdf`).
- `getCik()` only ever checked `company_tickers.json` (SEC's primary, operating-company-oriented ticker file). Added a **lazy** fallback to `company_tickers_mf.json` (the fund/series/class ticker file — "mf" = mutual fund, but shares the series/class registration structure most ETFs use) that only fires on a primary-map miss, so it adds **zero extra SEC calls** for the overwhelming majority of tickers that already resolve fine through the primary map.
- **Unverified against SEC's actual live files** — written from documented file-format knowledge (the same `{fields:[...], data:[[...]]}` shape as the sibling `company_tickers_exchange.json`), not a direct inspection. Parsed defensively (field lookup by name, not hardcoded position) and fails safe to `null` on any shape mismatch.
- Also worth knowing going in: `PRE_GATE_FORMS` is `8-K,10-Q,10-K` — operating-company forms a fund like DRAM will never file — so this fix changes the note from "No SEC CIK found" to a clean GREEN pass-through ("No solvency/dilution/guidance-cut language found"), not to an active RED/YELLOW trigger. That's the expected, correct outcome — Pre-Gate's trigger categories are operating-company risk concepts that don't really apply to a passively-tracked ETF.

## Test plan
- [x] `node --input-type=module --check` on `server.js`
- [ ] Confirm live after deploy: analyze DRAM and check that Pre-Gate's note changes from "No SEC CIK found" to a clean pass-through note, and check Render logs for any `getCikFromFundMap` errors
- [ ] If DRAM still doesn't resolve (e.g. if `company_tickers_mf.json` genuinely doesn't cover it either, being this recently listed), a small hardcoded override map would be a reasonable stopgap — not added preemptively here since it's unverified whether it's even needed

## Summary

- Adds `vcfa.tenant.deployment.list` (`GET /iaas/api/deployments`) as a typed read on the VCFA tenant plane, mirroring `vcfa.tenant.project.list` exactly — same plane, same OData `$filter`/`$orderby`/`$top`/`$skip` params, same `{content, totalElements, totalPages}` envelope. This is the tenant-plane inventory answer to "which deployments exist / which failed / which are stuck", the first read when a tenant reports "my deployment didn't come up".
- VCFA ships no ingestible spec, so the ingested `GET:/iaas/api/deployments` op is dispatch-inert on a real deploy — typed conversion is the only working read path (same rationale as the existing 5 typed ops). The handler is a pure pass-through GET, so vendor field shapes (`id`, `name`, `status`, `projectId`, `blueprintId`, `resources[]`, …) round-trip unchanged and set-shaped responses ride the dispatcher's existing JSONFlux result-handle seam, identical to `project.list`.
- A status `$filter` (e.g. `"status eq 'CREATE_FAILED'"`) narrows to failed deployments directly, the same way `project.list`'s `$filter` narrows to a named project.
- Refreshes `docs/codebase/connectors-vcf-automation.md`: adds the op to the typed table (now six) and retires the stale `core_ops.py` / `VcfaCoreGroup` / `VcfaCoreOp` / "Operator-review curation (G3.6-T11 #836)" sections to reflect the #2362 ingested-curation retirement.

author: heromoon9218
body:
第 1 章のレビューで挙がった 5 点に対応しました。うち 2 点は事実誤認、1 点は UI の不具合です。

## 事実誤認の修正

### `go mod init` が書く `go` ディレクティブ

「1.26 の `go mod init` は 1 つ前のマイナーバージョン（`go 1.25.0`）を書く」は **誤り** でした。手元の go1.26.5 で実測すると `go 1.26.5` が書かれます。

```
$ go mod init example.com/m
module example.com/m

go 1.26.5
```

Go 1.21 以降、`go mod init` は走っているツールチェインのバージョンをパッチまでそのまま書きます（`cmd/go/internal/modload/init.go` の `addGoStmt(modFile, ..., gover.Local())`）。パッチまで入るのは、`go` ディレクティブの意味が 1.21 で「言語バージョンの目印」から「ビルドに必要な最小ツールチェインの要求」に変わったためです。言語バージョンを決めるのは `1.26` の部分だけなので、`new(expr)` などはそのまま使えます（「手で書き換えが必要」という記述も誤りでした）。

なお「1 つ前」という話自体は Go に実在しますが別物で、`go mod tidy` の `-compat` の既定値が「`go` ディレクティブが示すバージョンの 1 つ前」です（ `go help mod tidy` ）。おそらくここと混線した記述でした。

修正箇所は ch01 の note・`go.mod` 例・章末問題 c1q2 と、同じ誤りが伝播していた **ch24 の c24q8** です。

### 復習キュー

CLAUDE.md で意図的に廃止したと明記されている機能の説明が本文に残っていました（ch01・ch24 の 2 箇所）。実際の挙動 — コード演習が中心で、Playground で試せない章だけ選択式 — に書き換えています。

## 表現の修正

- **DAG**: 1 章の初出でいきなり略語を使っていました（章末の解説では展開しているのに本文が先に略語を出している）。「有向非巡回グラフ」を展開し、なぜ並列コンパイルに効くかまで書きました。
- **単一バイナリに静的リンク**: 何と比べて配布が容易なのかが書かれていませんでした。JVM や Python 処理系との対比に言い換えています。
- **`go` ディレクティブの説明が note と `p` 段落で重複** していたので note に統合し、`go.mod — バージョンを明示する例` のコードブロックを削除しました。消した段落にあった「要求する最小の**言語**バージョン」という説明自体も 1.21 以降は不正確（正しくは最小の**ツールチェイン**バージョン）だったので、統合の際に直しています。`toolchain` 行の説明は第 12 章の表にあるため情報は欠けていません。

## 不具合の修正 — 「章を終える」が無反応

`ExerciseSection` の `onNext` が根本原因でした。

```js
} else {
  setCelebrated(true);   // ← 直前の onSolved で既に true。再描画すら起きない
}
```

完了パネルは `allDone && celebrated` でしか描画されないため、

- ステッパーで飛ばして未クリアが残っていると、押しても永久に何も起きない
- 全問クリア済みでもパネルは既にページ下部にあるだけで、スクロールもしないので「押しても無反応」に見える

`FinalsClient`（`/exam`）が同じ `ExerciseRunner` を使っていて、最後の演習では `onNext` に else 節すらなく **完全に無反応** だったため同時に直しました。

- 未クリアが残っていればその演習へ送る
- 全部クリア済みなら完了パネル（`#chapter-done` / `#finals-done`）へスクロール
- 演習が残っているのに「章を終える」と名乗らないよう、ラベルを `allDone` に連動。`/exam` 側は `lastLabel` で「総合演習を終える」に

## 検証

- `npm run typecheck` 通過
- `npm run build` 通過（全 24 章の SSG 31 ページ）
- 演習ファイルは変更していないため `verify-exercises.mts` は未実行

author: kyle-falconer
body:
Closes #420. Stacked on #427 — merge that first, then this retargets to `main` cleanly.

ADR-0056 fixes **two recipes per Item kind**. The parity recipes landed in #418/#419; this ratifies
the other half, so Phase 4 has something to build toward. All twelve open questions were walked
through and ruled on; the full table is on #420.

## Two parity claims that do not hold

Ratifying the targets meant checking the claims the parity seed rests on, and two failed.

**`PersistenceSeed` justifies its Habit/Event arm with "habits and events are never overdue".** Two
shipped readings say otherwise:

- `resolveOccurrenceState` gives a past unresolved firing `Missed` on an Active definition and
  `Skipped` on a shelved one, with **no kind branch anywhere**. A missed Habit day, Chore day and
  Event day are treated identically; the discriminator is the definition's light switch.
- `RecurrenceCursor` renders a missed Habit as overdue since the day its cursor stopped advancing,
  pinned in `RecurrenceCursorTest` against live item #277.

So `SkippedIfMissed` on a live definition was the **parity** answer, not the behaviour change ADR-0056
warned about — that warning rested on *"nothing logs a miss today"*, which fails under the model's own
*store the evidence, derive the label* rule. A miss that is derived and rendered is what "logged" has
to mean here.

Underneath sat the real finding: **`PersistencePolicy` runs two independent questions together.**
*What does the past day show* is computed on-device and kind-blind. *Does the undone thing follow me
into today* is still **fetched** — `refreshPlan` pulls the day's snapshot and full-replaces, so the
client caches a server-derived answer, which offline-first rules out. The kind-derived bit describes
only the second; #428 ports it the way `nextDeadlineAfter` ports cadence advancement.

**The per-doing aspect was never reachable.** `Dynamics.scope` is `Scope.Definition`, so
`Occurrence.validate()` rejects a bound and `Occurrence.aspect()` can only ever return `Process`. The
two-level reading ADR-0055 justifies the family with — *"a `Habitual` item whose every doing is a
`Performance`"* — has no second level. `ReadingsTest` was asserting `Aspect.Performance` on an
`Occurrence` that `validate()` refuses, passing only because it never called `validate()`. That test
now pins the real state; #429 closes the gap.

## What's here

**`recipe/TargetRecipe.kt`** — the ratified target for all eight Families, beside `ParityRecipe`.
Five targets are *identical to parity* and are recorded so that is a decision rather than an omission.
Three change, and each names its user-visible consequence at its declaration.

It deliberately **does not implement `KindRecipe`**: three targets cannot round-trip against the
four-kind wire, so the interface would be a type asserting something false. It grows into that
interface one Family at a time, which is ADR-0056's own sequencing.

**`TargetRecipeTest.kt`** — pins each target against the shipped reading it was justified by. The
load-bearing assertion is that `persistenceAtHorizon` agrees with `resolveOccurrenceState` arm for
arm, so the model cannot drift back into contradicting the interface. The parity divergence is pinned
as a set, so it cannot widen unnoticed.

**ADR-0056 amendment** — the fixture-trap premise. The caution still stands for `CreatesFollowUp`.

**ADR-0055 amendment** — Persistence is two axes; the per-doing bound has no home yet.

## User-visible changes named

Three targets diverge from parity in a way a person would notice, and each is called out where it is
declared:

- **`all_day` cleanup** (#433) — an Event that shows a time today may stop showing one
- **Lifecycle re-cut** — `Dropped` and `Archived` collapse, and terminality moves to the firing, so a
  finished item's *definition* reads `Active`
- **`DegradesIntoState`** — accepting a degrade unloads the item's recurrence rule, which
  `unfoldingProblems` forces rather than chooses

The Persistence reseed is visible-change-free: it stops the model contradicting what the UI already
renders.

## No production behaviour changes

`TargetRecipe` has no callers, exactly as `ParityRecipe` has none until the read facade lands. This
issue produced decisions and follow-up issues; #428 · #429 · #430 · #431 · #432 · #433 ·
Circuit-Stitch/Deferno#659 · Circuit-Stitch/Deferno#660.

## Gates

`:core:model:jvmTest` and `:koverVerify` green, real exit 0. `iosSimulatorArm64` + `macosArm64`
compiled separately — a JVM-only gate cannot see an Apple export collision on the new
`@ObjCName("PluginTargetRecipe")`.

author: khwilliamson
body:
Locale information was originally global for an entire process. Later, it was realized that different threads could want to be running in different locales. Windows added this ability, and POSIX 2008 followed suit (though using a completely different API). When available, perl automatically uses these capabilities.

But many platforms have neither, or their implementation, such as on Darwin, is buggy. This commit adds the capability for Perl programs to operate as if the platform were thread-safe.

This implementation is based on the observation that the underlying locale matters only to relatively few libc calls, and only during their execution. It can be anything at all at any other time. perl keeps what the proper locale should be for each category in a a per-thread array. Each locale-dependent operation must be wrapped in mutex lock/unlock operations. The lock additionally compares what libc knows the locale to be, and what it should be for this thread at this time, and changes the actual locale to the proper value if necessary. That's all that is needed.

This commit adds macros to perl.h, for example "MBTOWC_LOCK_", that expand to do the mutex lock, and change the global locale to the expected value. On perls built without this emulation capability, they are no-ops. All code in the perl core (unless I've missed something), are changed to use these macros (there weren't actually many places that needed this). Thus, any pure perl program will automatically become locale-thread-safe under this Configuration.

In order for XS code to also become locale-thread-safe, it must use these macros to wrap calls to locale-dependent functions. Relatively few modules call such functions. For example, the only one I found that ships with the perl core is Time::Piece, and it has more fundamental issues with running under threads than this. I am preparing pull requests for it.

Thus, this is not completely transparent to code like native-thread-safe locale handling is. Therefore ${^SAFE_LOCALES} returns 2 (instead of 1) for this type of thread-safety.

Another deficiency compared to the native thread safety is when a thread calls a non-perl library that accesses the locale. The typical example is Gtk (though this particular application can be configured to not be problematic). With the native safe threads, everything works as long as only one such thread is used per Perl program. That thread would then be the only one operating in the global locale, hence there are no conflicts. With this emulation, all threads are operating in the global locale, and mutexes would have to be used to prevent conflicts. To minimize those, the code added in this commit restores the global locale when through to the state it was in when started.

A major concern is the performance impact. This is after all trading speed for accuracy. lib/locale_threads.t is noticeably slower when this is being used. But that is doing multiple threads constantly using locale-dependent operations. I don't notice any change with the rest of the test suite. In pure perl, this only comes into play while in the scope of 'use locale' or when using some of the few POSIX:: functions that are locale-dependent. And to some extent when formatting, but the regular overhead there should dwarf what this adds.

This commit leaves this feature off by default.

* This set of changes does require a perldelta entry.

author: jeremyjpj0916
body:
## Summary
- Restore every hosted eBPF build after `bpf-linker 0.11.0` source installs stopped finding a compatible `llvm-config`.
- Replace mutable host-LLVM source builds with the official architecture-specific v0.11.0 static releases.
- Verify the upstream release assets against repository-pinned SHA-256 digests before installation in both Docker and GitHub Actions.

## Root-cause evidence
Two independent hosted paths fail before Ferrum eBPF compilation:
- [Ambient host-UDP production image job 94169608700](https://github.com/ferrum-edge/ferrum-edge/actions/runs/31613075992/job/94169608700)
- [NodeWaypoint eBPF live job 94168128677](https://github.com/ferrum-edge/ferrum-edge/actions/runs/31612669592/job/94168128677)

Both run `cargo install bpf-linker --locked`; v0.11.0 now defaults to `llvm-sys 231.0.0-rc2` and aborts because the runner or `rust:latest` image does not expose `llvm-config`. Upstream explicitly recommends its prebuilt release rather than `cargo install` because source installation depends on a specific mutable LLVM and system-library combination.

## Changes
- Add a fail-closed `setup-bpf-linker` composite action for Linux amd64/arm64. It validates version and digest formats, downloads only the pinned official archive, verifies SHA-256, and installs only the expected `bpf-linker` entry.
- Use that action in the ordinary eBPF build, live-kernel eBPF test, and NodeWaypoint live workflow.
- Make the multi-platform Docker eBPF builder select and verify the matching amd64/arm64 release archive.
- Update CI, Docker, and node-agent documentation to describe the immutable linker provenance.

## Test plan
- [x] `git diff --check`
- [ ] GitHub-hosted production eBPF Docker target downloads and executes the verified linker, builds the BPF ELF, and builds `runtime-ebpf-tools`.
- [ ] GitHub-hosted NodeWaypoint live workflow installs the verified linker and reaches the eBPF build/datapath checks.
- [ ] Ordinary hosted CI remains green.

No local Rust, build, test, Docker, or project commands were run; GitHub-hosted CI is the only execution gate.

body:
## Summary

- **Problem:** Stock Plannotator annotate ends the HTTP server on Close (`/api/exit` → `resolveDecision` → `stopServer`), so sharing a live review URL is unsafe for teams — one Close kills everyone.
- **Why it matters:** Archon `plannotator_gate` (and any multi-browser review) needs a live session where teammates can leave without ending the gate process.
- **What changed:**
  - Opt-in CLI flag `--persist-session` and server option `persistSession`
  - `POST /api/exit` with flag returns `{ ok: true, keptAlive: true }` and does **not** resolve `waitForDecision`
  - UI honors `keptAlive` (no “session ended” completion overlay)
  - Docs for annotate flags
- **What did not change:** Default lifecycle without the flag; Approve and Send Annotations still end the session

**Companion:** Archon PR https://github.com/anhle128/Archon/pull/33 uses this flag when spawning annotate.

## Behavior matrix

| Action | Default | `--persist-session` |
|--------|---------|---------------------|
| Close | dismissed + stop | keep server alive |
| Approve | approved + stop | same |
| Send Annotations | annotated + stop | same |

## Validation

```bash
bun test packages/server/annotate.test.ts apps/hook/server/cli.test.ts
# 47 pass (Task 1); UI/docs commit follows
```

- [ ] Close → server still serves URL; second browser can open it

- [ ] Without flag, Close still ends session

author: lodgvideon
body:
Closes #518.

## The question

`hpack`'s encoder passes `huffman=false` unconditionally
(`hpack/encoder.go:147,149`), while the sibling codec applies a shorter-wins
heuristic (`qpack/encoder.go:357,371`). #518 asked whether that asymmetry is
deliberate or a gap, and noted the answer was only inferable from a parameter
nothing but tests passes `true`.

(The issue cited lines 131/133 at `e5b9338`; they have drifted to 147/149. The
code is unchanged.)

## Answer: policy, and now it is measured

RFC 7541 §5.2 makes Huffman optional for a sender, so both codecs are conformant,
and this decoder honours the H bit either way.

The measurement that decides it is **per request on a warm connection**, which is
where a load generator spends essentially all of its time. Measuring a pile of
literals in isolation answers a much more flattering question.

| regime | bytes saved | CPU |
|---|---:|---|
| warm, fixed path | **0** — every field is an index, nothing is literal | unchanged |
| warm, varying `:path` | 15 (52→37) | 3.1 ns → **105 ns** per request |
| cold, first request on a connection | 95 (362→267) | 27 ns → **727 ns**, once |

Five runs per arm; within-arm spread 1.7–2.1%, so the deltas are far outside the
noise. Both arms are **0 allocs/op**.

## Why the 26% is real and still not worth taking

The saving on literals is genuine — every literal in the set compresses, 19.7% to
29.1%. What decides it is *where those bytes sit*. #438 profiled this exact
workload:

- syscalls **61.7%** of CPU, socket writes alone **44.2%**
- the whole HPACK encode: **1.4%**
- a warm 7-field request set encodes to **7 bytes**, because everything is indexed

Fewer bytes per write does not remove a write, and the write count is the cost.
That is the same reasoning that got precoded static header blocks **refuted** in
#438, measured rather than argued.

So on the primary regime the trade is: +102 ns per request (≈0.17% of a 61 µs
round trip) to save bytes on a path whose bottleneck is syscall count.

## What would overturn it

Recorded in the doc comment, because neither is hypothetical:

- **a bandwidth-constrained link**, where header bytes stop being free;
- **fidelity** — if the point is to exercise the server's Huffman decoder the way
  real clients do. That argues for an encoder *option*, not a new default, and is
  a separate ticket if anyone wants it.

## What changed

No behaviour. The policy is now stated on `Encoder`, where a reader meets it,
with the numbers and the conditions for revisiting; `encodeStringLiteral`'s
`huffman` parameter is documented as the switch and as what the decoder
round-trip tests drive, so it does not read as dead code and get "cleaned up".

`hpack/huffman_policy_test.go` keeps the measurement in the repo so the decision
is auditable and re-runnable rather than a claim in a commit message. Adopting
the heuristic later stays a two-line change that remains allocation-free.

## Verification

`go vet` clean, `golangci-lint run ./hpack/` 0 issues, `hpack` green under
`-race`, whole tree green under `-race`. No hpack benchmark allocates, so the
absolute bench gate (0 B/op, 0 allocs/op on `frame` + `hpack`) still holds with
the two new ones added.

author: oreginal
body:
Groundwork for the `/store` redesign. The Shopify catalogue isn't populated — `/store` renders three
products, which is too few to judge any layout against. This adds a local development catalogue
behind an environment switch so the storefront can be finished now and moved onto real products
later without a second redesign.

Closes #68.

## The switch

| `NEXT_PUBLIC_USE_PLACEHOLDER_PRODUCTS` | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `true` | development catalogue |
| `false` | Shopify |
| unset / anything else | Shopify |

Only the exact string `true` enables it, so a typo or a missing value can never serve fake products.
It's honoured in `getProducts` **and** `getProductBySlug`, so the home grid, the store and
`/store/[slug]` never disagree about which catalogue they're looking at — without the second one,
every development card would 404 the moment anyone clicked it.

`NEXT_PUBLIC_*` is inlined at **build** time. Flipping it in Netlify needs a **new build**;
redeploying an existing one keeps the old value baked in.

## The bug this PR found in itself

The first implementation put the entire development catalogue into `.next/static` — the **client**
bundle. Fourteen fake products downloaded by every visitor. Never rendered, but shipped.

It only happened with the flag **unset**, which is the documented safe default and what a fresh clone
has, so it was the common case. With the flag `false` the guarded `import()` is statically dead and
gets dropped, which is exactly why the first check looked clean. With it unset the comparison can't
be folded, the branch stays reachable, and the catalogue travels with it.

The cause was structural: four `"use client"` components — the card, the store grid, the featured
grid and the detail page — imported from `lib/shopify`, so the whole Storefront fetch layer was
already in the client graph.

Fixed by splitting along the seam the brief asked for, *keep data fetching separate from
presentation*:

- **`src/lib/product.ts`** — the `ShopifyProduct` shape and pure helpers (`isSoldOut`, `toCartItem`,
  `defaultVariant`, `getRelatedProducts`, `displayTags`, `getShowcaseProducts`). Safe anywhere.
- **`src/lib/shopify.ts`** — Storefront queries, `toProduct`, the fetchers, the switch. Server only.

Client components now import `lib/product` and cannot reach the queries or the catalogue behind them.
This also removed a `shopify → placeholder-products → shopify` import cycle that would have left
`FEATURED_TAG` in its TDZ when the catalogue's array literal evaluated.

**No parallel product type was introduced.** `ShopifyProduct` was already the shared model and still
is; the development catalogue simply satisfies it.

## Featured selection

`ShopifyProduct.featured` doesn't exist, and adding a field or a second interface was out of scope, so
selection is a pure selector over data that already exists. Products carrying the plain Shopify tag
`featured` come first — merchandiser-controlled from admin with no deploy, one mechanism for both
sources — then a deterministic top-up in catalogue order, which for Shopify is `sortKey: BEST_SELLING`.
Never random.

`toProduct` now keeps the raw tag list whole; it previously sliced to three, which could drop the
marker before `isFeatured` ever saw it. The three-tag cap moved to `displayTags`, which is a card
concern, and which also stops `featured` rendering as a visible chip.

## The catalogue is deliberately awkward

Not visual filler — it exists to exercise the real components. 14 products across Supplements /
Protein / Beauty / Wellness / Recovery, including single and multi variants, discounts and full
prices, a fully sold-out product, missing ratings, missing badges, cents (`R 219,99`), and names long
enough to test card wrapping.

One product — **Radiance Marine Collagen** — has its cheapest variant sold out while a pricier one is
discounted. That's the exact case #62's per-variant `compareAtPrice` fix targets, and the real store
still has no product that reproduces it. It now renders `R 749` with an `R 899` strikethrough, so
that fix finally has a live test.

## Verification

All three modes were built and served (`next start`, not `next dev`).

**`=true`** — 13/13 automated checks: 14 products on `/store`, all 14 detail pages 200, homepage on
the same catalogue, `R 219,99` cents and whole-rand formatting, sale strikethrough, sold-out pill, no
`Coming Soon` leak, no `featured` chip, unknown slug still 404s. Zero Shopify fetches during the
build.

**`=false`** — zero product links, no development names, development slug 404s, and **0 files**
containing catalogue data in either `.next/static` or the executable server JS.

**unset** — identical to `false` behaviourally, **0 files** in the client bundle. The module remains
in the *server* graph, unreachable behind a false condition; setting the flag explicitly to `false`
removes it there too, which is what `.env.example` recommends for production.

`npx tsc --noEmit` clean, `npm run images:check` passes (48 components). `npm run lint` is **not** a
gate — pre-existing breakage on `main` (#52, `next lint` removed in Next 16), not a regression here.

One process note: an early run showed `/store/radiance-marine-collagen` 404ing. It was a stale
artifact, not a defect — a live `next start` holds `.next` open on Windows, so `rm -rf .next` silently
partially failed and left a 404 page from the previous unset-mode build. The giveaway was that its
`.meta` carried the `products` cache tag, which only the Shopify path sets. It does not reproduce on a
clean build.

## Not in this PR

The store redesign itself (next PR). Shopify-backed bundles (#65), pagination past 50 (#64), the
wishlist/cart id mismatch (#63), category routes. No changes to Shopify auth, webhook logic or
`/api/revalidate`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

author: hieuslecong
body:
## Summary

Repairs `OASIS-RC-v2-reconstructed` for controlled true-normal RGB supervision and closes the reproducibility/fairness blockers found during full-repo audit.

### Data / Gate 0
- literal `is_normal: true/false`; true normals use `mask=null` virtual zero targets
- crack rows missing masks fail; crack rows remain crack even if a resized tensor becomes empty
- Gate 0 checks native and resized foreground and blocks cracks that disappear at the effective resolution
- raw + decoded RGB hashes, raw + decoded binary-mask hashes, decoded RGB-mask pair hashes
- repeated masks/pairs across splits are surfaced
- split-qualified lineage is rejected
- mismatched native image/mask resolution requires `alignment_verified=true` after a GT-only audit; same aspect ratio alone is not certification
- external normal manifest defaults to all-train if parent identity is unresolved; `normal_val` requires parent/session grouping through `--lineage-regex`
- canonical val/test row hashes are preserved when normals are appended

### Four-arm fairness
- S0 Control: `L_seg`
- S1 OASIS-RC-v2: `L_seg + lambda_oasis * rc_ramp * L_RCv2`
- S2 AOSK: `L_seg + lambda_aosk * L_AOSK`
- S3 combined: both intended auxiliaries
- AOSK is independent of RC warmup/ramp
- augmentation RNG and RC corruption RNG are independent; RC cannot shift later augmentations in S1/S3
- multi-step zero-weight contract test verifies control and connected updates remain bitwise equal when RC weight is zero
- official student arms require one exact `--student-init-checkpoint`
- S1/S3 require the same frozen `--critic-checkpoint`; inline critic training is debug-only
- strict `--deterministic` mode fails on nondeterministic PyTorch operations instead of warning

### True-normal critic semantics
- normal RGB + zero mask is a valid pair
- normal RGB + crack donor mask is an explicit invalid pair
- RGB-flip mismatch is only applied to crack-positive rows
- mask-flip mismatch is only scored when the mask actually changes
- corruption pair-valid targets are derived from the actual invalid map, so no-op corruptions are not forced invalid
- normal critic term has explicit `--normal-critic-weight` and no longer rescales the base critic objective

### Normal-fraction budget
- mixed batches have deterministic fixed composition
- requested fractions that round to zero normals fail instead of silently becoming N0
- optimizer steps per epoch are anchored to the crack-only baseline, so N25 does not get ~33% more updates than N0

### Diagnostics / provenance
- epoch-mean RC/AOSK loss logging
- `e_pred`, `e_gt`, `e_corrupted` and energy deltas
- weighted gradient norm/ratio/cosine diagnostic with fixed eval-mode student
- optional lineage-safe `normal_validation.json` false-positive diagnostics
- `effective_config.json` and `run_metadata.json` record exact command, git/runtime state, manifest/init/critic SHA256 and effective settings
- source hashes are generated at run time instead of relying on stale committed hashes

### Evaluation / scripts
- evaluator enforces student-only RGB checkpoint contract
- evaluator binds resolution to checkpoint unless explicit ablation is requested
- canonical GPU 256 configs for seeds 1337 / 2027 / 31415
- current `run_smoke.sh` runs validation-only S0/S1/S2/S3 with one shared critic and common init
- `run_three_seeds.sh` is paired and does not open test
- stale 128px evaluation wrapper and old reproduction instructions were replaced
- tracked `__pycache__`, `.pyc` and egg-info build metadata removed
- CI uses `requirements-tested.txt`, compileall, pytest and shell syntax checks

## Important scope

This PR deliberately does **not** change the reconstructed method-level formula `rank_gt = softplus(E_pred - E_gt + margin)`. Changing that is a scientific v2.1/ablation, not a bug fix, and must be selected using validation only.

## Local validation still required before merge

GitHub CI cannot access `/hdd1/...` or the A30. Before merge/run publication experiments:
1. run real-data Gate 0 at 256px;
2. perform GT-only review before setting any `alignment_verified=true`;
3. recover parent/session lineage if a normal_val split is wanted;
4. run local pytest + strict deterministic A30 micro-smoke;
5. require critic quality gate PASS;
6. run gradient diagnostics;
7. run validation-only N0/N25 and paired S0-S3 protocol;
8. keep canonical test unopened until the protocol is frozen.

The PR remains Draft until these local gates are closed.

author: matthis-k
body:
## Summary

Refactors `phenix-nvim` into a mini.nvim-style feature collection and makes Phenix ACP the sole agent/harness frontend.

### Feature collection

The repository now exports independently consumable plugins for:

- `phenix-ui`: shared frontend utilities and the typed Phenix API/config/state runtime
- `phenix-acp`: thin Neovim frontend wrapper for the Phenix ACP harness
- `phenix-bars`: statusline/tabline/statuscolumn composition
- `phenix-color-preview`: palette preview
- `phenix-picker`: picker/search/navigation frontend
- `phenix-session`: session lifecycle and picker bridge
- `phenix-theme`: theme/highlight integration
- `phenix-git`: Git integration
- `phenix-lsp`: LSP integration
- `phenix-completion`: completion integration
- `phenix-dashboard`: dashboard frontend
- `phenix-explorer`: explorer frontend
- `phenix-terminal`: terminal frontend
- `phenix-notify`: notification frontend

Basic editor options and final user key choices remain distribution policy rather than artificial feature plugins.

### Shared public facade

`phenix-ui` initializes one global Phenix facade with three parallel namespaces:

```lua
Phenix.config.<feature>
Phenix.api.<feature>
Phenix.state.<feature>
```

Every feature registration creates all three slots. Examples:

```lua
Phenix.config.git.refresh_interval = 60000
Phenix.api.git.refresh()
local session = Phenix.state.acp.session
```

`Phenix.api` is the public API/facade, not an interface registry. The shared runtime internally uses typed `PhenixApiSurface<T>` wrappers to bind implementations and validate runtime contracts. LuaLS/EmmyLua types define the concrete public surfaces (`PhenixUi`, `PhenixGit`, `PhenixLsp`, `PhenixPicker`, `PhenixBars`, `PhenixAcpFrontend`, etc.).

Feature configuration may be supplied before the feature loads by assigning `Phenix.config.<feature> = { ... }`; registration preserves the table and fills only missing defaults. Invalid namespace types and duplicate API ownership fail immediately instead of being silently replaced.

`Phenix.require_api(name)` exists only for dynamic fail-fast dispatch. Ordinary integrations can use the typed direct facade (`Phenix.api.git`, `Phenix.api.lsp`, and so on).

The shared UI plugin publishes `Phenix.api.ui`; the ACP frontend consumes its window utilities through that facade rather than importing a separate frontend implementation.

Distribution keymap descriptors now use semantic `{ api = "picker", method = "files" }` actions and resolve through the Phenix API facade rather than reaching directly into implementation plugins.

### Tight feature integration

- `phenix-bars` owns the actual Phenix statusline/tabline/statuscolumn surfaces, not just renderer primitives.
- Bars consume Git state through `Phenix.api.git`; Git owns its remote/status cache under `Phenix.state.git` and refresh policy under `Phenix.config.git`.
- `phenix-session` owns its Resession policy under `Phenix.config.session` and exposes session actions through `Phenix.api.session`.
- Color preview is configured through `Phenix.config.color_preview` and invoked through `Phenix.api.color_preview`.
- ACP settings are projected into the stable `Phenix.config.acp` table; the active session is projected into `Phenix.state.acp.session`.
- Feature API wrappers carry runtime contracts and LuaLS annotations.

### ACP replaces OpenCode

OpenCode is removed from the wrapped runtime, plugin dependencies, active mappings, and configuration. `phenix-acp` is the harness frontend and publishes its typed facade at `Phenix.api.acp`.

The ACP plugin exposes Lua plus `<Plug>` actions only. `setup()` configures the frontend without installing user mappings; the distribution maps `<leader>p`, `pf`, `pt`, `pm`, and `pc` to the public `<Plug>` actions.

### ACP responsiveness retained

The earlier transport hardening in this PR remains:

- coalesced stdout chunks with bounded scheduled drains
- independent error boundaries per decoded ACP frame
- callback/permission/exit handler isolation
- `session/cancel` support and follow-up clearing

The conductor-side acknowledgement/lock stall remains fixed separately in `matthis-k/phenix-agent-harness#286`.

### Testing

Startup coverage asserts:

- the global `Phenix.api` / `Phenix.config` / `Phenix.state` shape for every feature, including shared UI
- API lookup resolves to the same public facade objects
- OpenCode mappings are absent
- bars and color-preview are loaded through their feature plugins
- public ACP `<Plug>` actions exist
- the real ACP session becomes ready and is projected into `Phenix.state.acp.session`
- hiding/reopening the frontend preserves the ACP process
- a failing ACP notification handler cannot swallow a later response frame
